title: Title
notes: Open by explaining that this appendix is not being treated as a collection of numbers to memorize. The lecture turns spherical lookup tables into reproducible algorithms, so every value has a model, a statistic, parameters, and a numerical check attached to it.

title: Route
notes: Use this route slide to separate the appendix into four table-making tasks. Students should hear that Fisher cap radii, Fisher concentration estimates, Watson axial moments, and critical values answer different statistical questions and should not be mixed just because they appear in the same appendix.

title: Contract
notes: Frame the deck around a simple contract. A printed table value is only a final number, while a reproducible calculator exposes the geometry, model, statistic, computation, and diagnostic check that produced that number. This contract also tells students what information must appear in any report that cites a lookup.

title: Fisher Cap Quantile
notes: Make the first replacement geometric. A Fisher quantile table is not a generic probability chart; it reports the angular radius of a cap around a specified pole, so the output should be read in degrees or radians on the sphere.

title: Cap Radius Dashboard
notes: Use the curve family to show why a table can be replaced by a function. The important qualitative check is monotonicity: for any fixed probability level, higher concentration should produce a smaller cap radius. If a computed curve reverses that trend, the formula or units should be questioned before the value is used.

title: Fisher Concentration
notes: Explain that the concentration table is really an inverse function table. The executable notebook solves the equation directly and then recomputes A3 at the solution, so the residual becomes a compact audit of the lookup.

title: Resultant Calculations
notes: Pause on the resultant because it drives several spherical table entries. The sum of unit vectors gives both a direction and a length, but the direction becomes unstable when the length is small, so the diagnostic must be interpreted before it is passed into a Fisher calculator.

title: Watson Geometry
notes: Contrast Fisher and Watson visually before introducing any Watson lookup. The sign of Watson concentration changes the geometry, so a table user must know whether the application is directional, bipolar axial, or girdle-like. Ask learners to point to the relevant panel before they name a formula.

title: Watson Moment Lookup
notes: Explain that the Watson table is based on second-moment information along an axis. This is why it can detect structure that the resultant vector may miss, especially when antipodal or girdle patterns cancel the first moment.

title: Critical Values
notes: Connect critical values to the null model instead of treating them as magic constants. A simulation table is reproducible when it records the statistic, sample size, alpha level, random seed, and number of repetitions. Those details are what let another notebook rebuild the same reference distribution.

title: Critical Surface
notes: Use the surface to explain why interpolation is a statistical decision, not just a formatting task. If a requested sample size or alpha level is between printed entries, the reproducible response is to recompute or interpolate with the monotone behavior in view.

title: Numerical Checks
notes: Emphasize that diagnostics are part of the table replacement, not optional decoration. A calculator without a failure sensor can silently return a number under the wrong geometry, the wrong null, or a broken simulation. The check list is therefore a statistical claim about trust, not merely software hygiene.

title: Choosing The Calculator
notes: Turn the appendix into a decision table. The instructor can ask learners to identify the statistical question first, then read across the row to choose the geometry, statistic, calculator, and diagnostic check. This prevents the common habit of reaching for whichever row looks numerically close.

title: Failure Modes
notes: Use this slide as a quality-control checklist. The biggest danger is not arithmetic error; it is applying the right-looking table to the wrong geometric object or reporting a simulated threshold without enough information to reproduce it.

title: Mini Lab
notes: Keep the lab short and focused on routing. The point is not to calculate a final number on the slide, but to make learners say which calculator is appropriate and which diagnostic would prove the result was computed correctly.

title: Recap
notes: Close by returning to the contract: a lookup value is useful only when the geometry, model, statistic, computation, and check are still attached. That is the advantage of an executable appendix over a static printed table.
